issues.legal_issue: A binding compensation award made by a competent non-court authority is an order for purposes of determining court fees, even if it is not a civil court order or is not executable.
material_facts: A competent arbitrator determined the compensation payable for acquired property and issued a formal award binding on the parties.
The governing acquisition law required the competent authority to pay the compensation awarded.
The arbitrator was not a civil court, and the award was not shown to be executable.
issues.conclusion: The award was an order for purposes of the court-fee provision; its non-executability and lack of the force of a decree did not prevent that characterization.
issues.legal_principle: The applicable court-fee provision used the undefined term “order,” so the Court applied its ordinary meaning: a formal expression of a decision by a competent authority that binds the parties. The statutory requirement to pay the compensation supported the award’s effect; neither the absence of a civil-court order nor the question of execution was determinative.

rule.if: compensation_determination_proceeding and competent_authority_issued_formal_decision and decision_binds_parties and payment_of_award_required

predicates.compensation_determination_proceeding: The proceeding determines compensation payable for property that has been requisitioned or acquired.
predicates.competent_authority_issued_formal_decisi: A competent authority issued a formal decision determining compensation.
predicates.decision_binds_parties: The decision binds the parties to the proceeding.
predicates.payment_of_award_required: The applicable law requires the responsible authority to pay the compensation determined by the decision.

issues.definition: When a compensation-determination proceeding produces a formal, binding decision by a competent authority that the law requires to be paid, that decision counts as an order for fee purposes.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal concerning an order awarding compensation for land acquisition attracts ad valorem court fees, and the order need not have the force of a decree.
material_facts: The Special Deputy Collector appealed the arbitrator’s compensation award to the High Court.
The applicable court-fee law provided that the fee on an appeal against an order relating to acquisition compensation was computed by comparing the amount awarded with the amount claimed.
The appellant’s cross-objection sought compensation beyond the amount awarded.
issues.conclusion: The compensation appeal attracted ad valorem court fees under the applicable fee schedule; the court-fee provision did not require the order under appeal to have the force of a decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(1) of the Bombay Court-fee Act, 1959, was a computation provision, not a charging provision, and its comparison of the amount awarded with the amount claimed indicated an ad valorem fee under Schedule I rather than a fixed fee under Schedule II. The Court applied Anandalal Chakrabarti, which construed the corresponding provision of the Court-fee Act, 1870, and held that no requirement that the order have the force of a decree should be added to the statutory text.

predicates.appeal_concerns_compensation_award: A party appealed a decision determining compensation for acquired property.
predicates.compensation_claim_differs_from_award: The compensation claimed differs from the amount awarded.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a compensation award and the claimed amount differs from the award, the appeal bears an ad valorem fee.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent’s cross-objection seeking modification of an award outside the general arbitration law is, in substance, a memorandum of appeal chargeable with an ad valorem fee.
material_facts: The Special Deputy Collector appealed an arbitrator’s compensation award made under a law other than the Arbitration Act, 1940.
The appellant, as respondent to that appeal, filed a cross-objection seeking additional compensation and paid a fixed fee.
The cross-objection sought modification of the award to the extent the appellant was dissatisfied with it.
issues.conclusion: The cross-objection was a memorandum of appeal in substance and was chargeable with an ad valorem fee under Article 3 of Schedule I, not a fixed fee under Article 13 of Schedule II.
issues.legal_principle: Article 3 of Schedule I to the Bombay Court-fee Act, 1959, covered a petition, including a memorandum of appeal, seeking to set aside or modify an award made otherwise than under the Arbitration Act, 1940. A cross-objection is a form of appeal in substance because it allows a respondent to challenge the decision under appeal and takes the place of a cross-appeal. The Court applied Anandalal Chakrabarti and approved The Chatusshakhiya Brahmavrinda Gayaran Trust v. Union of India; it treated the omission of express reference to cross-objections in Article 3 as inartistic drafting.

rule.if: appeal_against_award and award_outside_general_arbitration_law and respondent_files_cross_objection and cross_objection_seeks_modification

predicates.appeal_against_award: A party has appealed a decision that determines compensation or otherwise makes an award.
predicates.award_outside_general_arbitration_law: The challenged award was made under a special legal regime rather than the general arbitration law.
predicates.respondent_files_cross_objection: A respondent to the appeal filed a cross-objection.
predicates.cross_objection_seeks_modification: The cross-objection seeks to change the award to the extent the respondent is dissatisfied with it.

issues.definition: When a respondent files a cross-objection seeking to modify an award made under a special legal regime in an appeal against that award, the cross-objection bears an ad valorem fee.
